4.2.10.title: Nonstandard extensions
4.2.10.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Nonstandard extensions are language elements or functionality in an implementation that consist of any of the following:'. Item 3: 'language elements defined in this Working Draft International Standard for which different functionality is implemented, where that language element is required for conformance ... provided that standard-conforming behavior is also implemented and that an implementor-defined mechanism exists for selection of the nonstandard behavior.' The items are not a bare index: each carries conditions with normative force ('standard support for that element is not claimed', 'provided that ... is also implemented') that determine what an implementation may treat as a nonstandard extension while conforming, and the definition is load-bearing for the trailing shall-requirements (documentation, warning mechanism) that reference 'nonstandard extensions' ⇒ normative. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: the items define the meaning of a conformance category, not the order in which words or elements may be written ⇒ GR (definitional list).

4.4.title: A conforming run unit
4.4.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'A conforming run unit is one that:'. Item 2: 'complies with the explicitly stated provisions and specifications of standard COBOL with respect to the runtime behavior of that run unit.' The items state the requirements an entity must satisfy to BE a conforming run unit — they define the meaning of the term and impose runtime-behavior compliance, so they are normative, not a bare index. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: nothing here constrains the order in which words or elements may be written; the items define the meaning of 'conforming run unit' and its runtime-behavior relationship to the standard ⇒ GR.

5.5.title: Integer operands
5.5.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Item 1: 'When the term ‘integer-n’ … is used in a general format and associated rules, it refers to a fixed-point integer literal that shall be unsigned and nonzero unless otherwise specified'. Item 2: 'When the term ‘integer’ is used as a constraint for an operand in a syntax rule, then … it shall be an integer literal'. Item 3: 'When the term ‘integer’ is used as a constraint for an operand in a general rule, that operand shall evaluate at runtime as follows'. All three state requirements ('shall') ⇒ normative. Kind test: items 1 and 2 restrict what may be WRITTEN where the term appears (an unsigned nonzero literal; an integer literal or a data item whose description has no digits right of the radix point) — §5.3.2 restrictions on elements as written ⇒ SR. Item 3 explicitly governs runtime evaluation ('shall evaluate at runtime', native vs standard arithmetic) — §5.3.3 execution semantics ⇒ GR. Kinds differ ⇒ mixed-kinds.

6.1.title: General
6.1.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'The following rules apply to the indicated reference formats:' — the clause itself names them rules. Item 1b: 'A COBOL compiler shall accept source text and library text written in reference format.' Item 2a: 'A COBOL compiler shall process fixed-form reference format lines as though the lines had been logically converted from fixed form to free form'. Item 3a: 'The number of character positions on a line may vary from line to line, ranging from a minimum of 0 to a maximum of 255.' These state requirements on the processor and restrictions on source form ⇒ normative. Kind is not uniform: items 1 and 2 are processor obligations and treatment-during-analysis clarifications ('the first character-string of a compilation group is treated as though it were preceded by a separator space') — §5.3.3's 'defines or clarifies the meaning ... and the effect that it has on either execution or compilation' fits; they do not constrain the order in which words may be written. Item 3 restricts how a free-form line may be written (0–255 character positions; implementor-specified line-terminating control characters and whether they may appear in comments and literals) — §5.3.2's 'impose restrictions on individual words or elements' / how source may be written ⇒ SR. Not all one kind ⇒ mixed-kinds.

6.3.4.title: Program-text area
6.3.4.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'The program-text area may contain:'. Item 2: 'Any of the following or combinations of the following, subject to further syntax specifications, when the indicator area contains a continuation indicator or a source indicator'. Each item states a permission about what may be WRITTEN in the program-text area, conditioned on the indicator-area content — a closed list of permitted source contents, so it carries normative force (an area content outside the list is not permitted). §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: these constrain where/how source text may be written in the reference format (compile-time well-formedness of lines), not the meaning of any construct ⇒ SR.

6.3.5.title: Continuation of lines
6.3.5.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Continuation of an alphanumeric, boolean, or national literal is indicated when either:'. Item 1: 'A line terminates within an alphanumeric or boolean literal without a closing delimiter and the next line that is not a comment line or a blank line contains a fixed continuation indicator'. The items state the conditions under which continuation of a literal is indicated in source text — normative recognition conditions, not a bare index. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: these govern how source elements may be WRITTEN across lines and how the written form is analyzed at compile time (reference format, clause 6), i.e. compile-time well-formedness of written text, not execution meaning ⇒ SR.

6.5.title: Logical conversion
6.5.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'The resultant logically-converted compilation group is created in free-form reference format as follows:'. Item 2: 'If the line is a comment line or a blank line, that line is logically discarded.' The nine items are the required algorithm every conforming compiler applies to convert fixed-form to free-form; they define the effect of SOURCE FORMAT directives, comment lines, continuation indicators, etc. => normative. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: they do not constrain the order in which the programmer may write words or elements — they define the MEANING/EFFECT of what was written (what each line kind becomes in the resultant compilation group), i.e. they 'define or clarify the meaning' of reference-format constructs => GR.

7.2.2.5.title: Text-words
7.2.2.5.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'A text-word is a character-string, other than a comment or the COBOL word 'COPY', in source text or in library text that constitutes an element processed by text manipulation. A text-word may be one of the following:'. Item 1: 'a separator, except for: a space; a pseudo-text delimiter; and the opening and closing delimiters for alphanumeric, boolean, and national literals. In determining which character sequences form text-words, the colon, the right parenthesis, and the left parenthesis characters ... are treated as separators'. These define which character sequences constitute text-words — the unit on which COPY/REPLACE matching operates — so they carry normative force (they decide what REPLACING can and cannot match), not a bare index ⇒ normative. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: the items define the MEANING of 'text-word' (a definitional list of its three forms); they do not constrain the order in which words or elements may be written ⇒ GR. (Item 3's implementor permission 'The implementor may prohibit the use of one or more characters from outside the COBOL character repertoire in, or as, text-words' is still part of the definitional item, not a written-order constraint.)

8.1.2.title: Computer's coded character set
8.1.2.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'The COBOL specification is independent of the encoding used to represent a computer's coded character set, except that:'. Item 1: 'The number of bytes used in the memory of the computer to represent characters in the alphanumeric coded character set shall be the same for all characters in that coded character set; the number of bytes shall be determined at compile time.' Each item is a 'shall' requirement — clearly normative. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: the items constrain the runtime/memory representation of the coded character sets (byte counts, fixed-width, national >= alphanumeric), not where or how source text may be written ⇒ GR.

8.3.2.1.title: General
8.3.2.1.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Within a source element the following apply:'. Item 1: 'Reserved words shall not be used as user-defined words or system-names.' Item 5: 'Intrinsic-function-names may be used as user-defined words and system-names, except for …'. Each item states a prohibition or permission on word use ⇒ normative rules. §5.3.2 test: they 'impose restrictions on individual words' — which classes of COBOL words may be written as user-defined words or system-names in source text, a compile-time well-formedness constraint, not execution meaning ⇒ SR for all five.

8.3.2.2.title: User-defined words
8.3.2.2.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29) with PER-SUBLIST kinds, the mechanism DEVLOG 1166 said this clause needs. All five sub-lists are normative; they are not all one kind. Sub-list 1 ('a given user-defined word may be used as only one type of user-defined word with the following exceptions') and sub-list 3 ('Externalized names shall be referenced in a source element only:') constrain where words may be WRITTEN in source text - SR per SS5.3.2. Sub-list 2 ('The following user-defined words shall be externalized to the operating environment:') states an operating-environment effect, and sub-lists 4 and 5 (the INVOKE method-name and CALL/CANCEL program-name naming-convention lists, 'that method-name is treated as ...') state treatment/meaning - GR per SS5.3.3. Sub-list indices follow the extractor's segmentation: the first list is sublist 1 (plain ids), the remaining four are L2..L5 in document order.

8.3.2.4.2.title: Required words
8.3.2.4.2.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'A required word is a word whose presence is required when the format in which the word appears is used. Required words are of two types:'. Item 1: 'Keywords. Within each format, such words are uppercase and underlined.' Item 2: 'Special character words. The special character words are:' followed by the table assigning each special character word its meaning (e.g. '== | Pseudo-text delimiter in COPY and REPLACE statements'). These define the terms keyword and special character word and bind the presence-required convention that every general format relies on ⇒ normative, not a bare index. §5.3.2 test: syntax rules 'define a term that may be used in the remaining syntax rules' and govern how words 'may be written to form larger elements' — these items define exactly such format-notation terms and constrain what must be written when a format is used; they do not define execution meaning per §5.3.3 ⇒ SR.

8.3.3.3.2.title: Fixed-point numeric literals
8.3.3.3.2.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'The rules for the formation and value of fixed-point numeric literals are as follows:' — the clause itself announces two rule species, formation and value. Item 1: 'A literal shall contain at least one digit.' Items 1-3 are 'shall'/'shall not' constraints on how the literal character-string is WRITTEN (digit presence, sign position, decimal-point position) ⇒ §5.3.2 written-order/form test ⇒ SR. Item 4: 'The value of a fixed-point numeric literal is the algebraic quantity represented by the characters in the fixed-point numeric literal.' — defines the meaning (value and size) of the literal ⇒ §5.3.3 meaning test ⇒ GR. Not all one kind ⇒ mixed-kinds. (Items 2 and 3 each end with a semantic consequence sentence — 'If the literal is unsigned, the literal is nonnegative'; 'The decimal point is treated as an assumed decimal point' — but each item's dominant force is the written-form constraint, so SR per item.)

8.3.3.3.3.title: Floating-point numeric literals
8.3.3.3.3.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'The rules for the formation and value of floating-point numeric literals are:' — the lead-in itself splits the list into FORMATION and VALUE. Items 1-4 constrain the written form ('The significand ... shall include a decimal point. The significand shall be from 1 to 36 digits in length', 'shall have a maximum of four digits and no decimal point', 'neither significand nor exponent shall have a negative sign') — §5.3.2 test: they constrain how the literal may be WRITTEN ⇒ SR. Item 5: 'The value of a floating-point numeric literal is the algebraic product of the value of its significand and the quantity derived by raising ten to the power of the exponent' — §5.3.3 test: defines the MEANING (value) of the literal ⇒ GR. Not all one kind ⇒ mixed-kinds.

8.3.5.title: Separators
8.3.5.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'A separator is one of the following, except when appearing in a literal:'. Item 3: 'The COBOL character period, when followed by a space, is a separator. The separator period shall be used only to indicate the end of a sentence, or as shown in formats.' Item 5: 'The opening delimiter shall be immediately preceded by a space, left parenthesis, or opening pseudo-text delimiter.' The items both define the separator inventory and impose shall/may-only constraints (balanced parentheses, required preceding spaces, where the period may be used) => normative. §5.3.2 test: every item constrains where and how characters and delimiters may be WRITTEN in source text — compile-time lexical well-formedness, not execution meaning => SR.

8.4.2.2.1.title: General
8.4.2.2.1.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Qualification of a user-defined name is required unless one of the following is true:' (and the preceding sentence: 'uniqueness shall be established through qualification for each user-defined name explicitly referenced, except as specified in rules 2 through 6' — the body itself calls these numbered items RULES). Item 1: 'No other name has the identical spelling.' Item 6: 'The name is a paragraph-name and the section containing the reference also contains the named paragraph.' Each item states a condition exempting a written reference from the qualification requirement ⇒ normative (requirement + enumerated exemptions). §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: the requirement governs what must be WRITTEN in a reference (qualifiers) for the source text to be well-formed — compile-time uniqueness of reference, checked before any execution semantics ⇒ SR for all six items.

8.4.6.2.1.title: General
8.4.6.2.1.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'When such a duplicated name is referenced in source element B, the following rules are used to determine the referenced item:' — the body itself calls them rules. Item 2: 'If only one item is identified, it is the referenced item.' The items determine which declared item a duplicated name resolves to, a requirement with force of its own — normative. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: they do not constrain the order in which words may be written; they define the MEANING (the referent) of a name reference across nested source elements ⇒ GR.

8.4.6.3.title: Scope of program-names
8.4.6.3.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'The following rules regulate the scope of a program-name for the CALL and CANCEL statements, and the program-address-identifier:'. Item 1: 'If the program-name is that of a program that does not possess the common attribute and that is directly contained within another program, that program-name may be referenced only by statements included in that containing program …'. The lead-in itself calls them rules, and each item states a permission/restriction ('may be referenced only by') ⇒ normative. §5.3.2 test: they restrict WHERE in the source a program-name may be written as a reference (which source elements may contain the referencing statement) — compile-time name-visibility well-formedness, not the runtime meaning of the reference ⇒ SR.

8.5.1.3.2.title: Level-numbers
8.5.1.3.2.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Three types of entries exist for which there is no true concept of level. These are:'. Item 1: 'Entries that specify elementary items or groups introduced by a RENAMES clause.' Item 3: 'Entries that specify condition-names.' The items are noun phrases, but jointly with the lead-in they assert the normative classification that these three entry types stand outside the level hierarchy — the exception invoked by the clause's opening ('There are special level-numbers, 66, 77, and 88, that are exceptions to this rule'), and this classification is asserted here, not elsewhere; the following paragraphs only add the 66/77/88 assignments ⇒ normative, not a bare index. §5.3.3 test: the items 'define or clarify the meaning or relationship of meanings' of the level-number organization (which entries carry no true level), not the order in which words may be written per §5.3.2 ⇒ GR.

8.5.1.4.title: Limitations of character handling
8.5.1.4.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'The following processing limitations shall apply when ISO/IEC 10646 is chosen as a computer's coded character set:'. Item 2: 'The high-half 2 octets and the low-half 2 octets of a four-octet sequence defined in the UTF-16 format of ISO/IEC 10646 are each treated as a single character position.' The lead-in says 'shall apply' and each item defines how characters are treated at runtime ⇒ normative. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: these define the runtime meaning of a character position under UTF-16 (processing semantics), not where or how source words may be written ⇒ GR.

8.5.1.6.4.title: Item alignment for increased object-code efficiency
8.5.1.6.4.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Synchronization is accomplished in two ways:'. Item 2: 'By recognizing the appropriate natural boundaries and organizing the data suitably without the use of the SYNCHRONIZED clause.' The items are complete statements defining HOW synchronization (defined just above: 'Data items that are aligned on these natural boundaries ... are defined to be synchronized') is accomplished; item 2's content lives nowhere else, so this is not a bare index whose normative content is elsewhere ⇒ normative. §5.3.3 test: they define/clarify the meaning of synchronization and how it is achieved — a definitional clarification of behavior, not a constraint on the order in which words may be written ⇒ GR.

8.5.1.9.1.title: General
8.5.1.9.1.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'A dynamic-capacity table differs from an occurs-depending table in that:'. Item 1: 'its occurrences are created dynamically,'; item 2: 'it may have an unlimited capacity,'; item 3: 'it may be defined in any place, other than the file section, in which a fixed-capacity table may be defined and may be nested in any combination to the same number of levels as a fixed-capacity table.' The items carry normative force of their own (a permission of unlimited capacity; a placement permission that excludes the file section) => rules, not prose enumeration. Kind test per item: items 1 and 2 define runtime behavior/meaning of the table concept (§5.3.3 'defines or clarifies the meaning') => GR; item 3 governs WHERE the table may be defined and how deeply nested it may be written in source — §5.3.2 written-placement territory => SR. Not all one kind => mixed-kinds.

8.5.1.9.6.title: Exceeding capacity
8.5.1.9.6.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'The creation of a new element in a dynamic-capacity table may result in one of the following exceptions:'. Item 1: 'The nonfatal EC-BOUND-OVERFLOW exception condition shall exist when a dynamic-capacity table has an expected capacity and an operation causes this expected capacity to be exceeded.' Item 2: 'The fatal EC-BOUND-TABLE-LIMIT exception condition shall exist when an operation attempts to increase the capacity of a dynamic-capacity table to a value higher than the maximum capacity of the table based on the resources available at runtime.' Both items carry 'shall exist when' — they define exception conditions and their runtime trigger and continuation semantics, the same shape as the admitted §14.7.5 size-error precedent ⇒ normative. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: they define when a runtime condition exists and what execution then does, not where words may be written ⇒ GR.

8.5.1.11.3.title: Availability and persistence of variable-length data items
8.5.1.11.3.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'The resources used by a variable-length data item may be freed automatically when:'. Item 4: 'the program containing the data item is a called program and a CANCEL is executed referring to it;'. The items are the operative conditions of a normative permission — they define exactly when the implementation is permitted to free the item's resources, so they carry normative force. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: these are execution-time events (finalization, EXIT PROGRAM, GOBACK, CANCEL, fatal exception, shrink, overwrite), defining runtime resource behavior, not written order of words ⇒ GR.

8.5.1.12.1.title: General
8.5.1.12.1.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Determination of compatibility between a variable-length group and another group is as follows:'. Item 1: 'For each dynamic-capacity table in either group there is a corresponding table in the other group as specified in 8.5.1.12.2, Positional correspondence.' The items jointly DEFINE when two groups are compatible — the term the clause then uses to permit or forbid moves and comparisons ⇒ normative. §5.3.3 test: they 'define or clarify the … relationship of meanings of an element or set of elements' (the compatibility relation between two groups), a definitional list, not a constraint on where words may be written ⇒ GR.

8.5.2.3.title: Alphanumeric category
8.5.2.3.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Each of the following is a data item of category alphanumeric:'. Item 2: 'An elementary data item described with a VALUE clause containing an alphanumeric literal, and without a PICTURE clause.' Item 4: 'An alphanumeric function.' Each item states a sufficient condition for category membership — a definitional rule the whole standard depends on ⇒ normative. §5.3.3 test: they 'define or clarify the meaning' of category alphanumeric (a definitional category list, same shape as the admitted §8.5.2.12 Numeric category precedent), not where or in what order words may be written per §5.3.2 ⇒ GR.

8.5.2.5.title: Boolean category
8.5.2.5.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Each of the following is a data item of category boolean:'. Item 3: 'A group item explicitly or implicitly described with a GROUP-USAGE clause with the BIT phrase.' Each item is a defining condition of category membership ('is a data item of category boolean') — normative definitional content, not a bare index of names. §5.3.3 test: the list defines the meaning of the boolean category (which items belong to it), not the order in which words may be written ⇒ GR. Matches the admitted precedent shape (category-definition lists are GR).

8.5.2.8.title: Index category
8.5.2.8.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Each of the following is a data item of category index:'. Item 1: 'An elementary data item explicitly or implicitly described as usage index.' The items define category membership ('is a data item of category index') — they define meaning, so they are normative, matching the admitted category-clause precedent. §5.3.3 test: a definitional list of what constitutes the index category defines the meaning of the category, not where words may be written ⇒ GR.

8.5.2.10.title: National category
8.5.2.10.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Each of the following is a data item of category national:'. Item 3: 'A group item explicitly or implicitly described with a GROUP-USAGE clause with the NATIONAL phrase.' The four items are the complete membership definition of the national category (closed by the closing sentence 'Such an item is referred to as a national data item.') => normative definitional list, the same shape as the admitted §8.5.2.12 Numeric category. §5.3.3 test: they define the meaning of 'category national' — category membership, not the order in which words may be written => GR (definitional category list).

8.5.2.12.title: Numeric category
8.5.2.12.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Each of the following is a data item of category numeric:'. Item 1: 'An elementary data item described as numeric by its PICTURE character-string and not described with a BLANK WHEN ZERO clause.' Item 2 enumerates the numeric usages (binary-char ... float-decimal-34); items 3-5 are LINE-COUNTER, LINAGE-COUNTER, PAGE-COUNTER; items 6-7 numeric and integer functions. Closing: 'Such an item is referred to as a numeric data item.' The items exhaustively define membership in category numeric, which every category-driven rule in the standard depends on ⇒ normative, not a bare index. §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: they define the meaning of a data category (a definitional category list), not the order in which words may be written ⇒ GR.

8.5.2.13.title: Numeric-edited category
8.5.2.13.why: ADMITTED 2026-08-08 (owner decision: adjudicate all 100, admit the normative ones; fix-queue PB29; reader+refuter batch). Lead-in: 'Each of the following is a data item of category numeric-edited:'. Item 2: 'A data item described as numeric by its PICTURE character-string and described with a BLANK WHEN ZERO clause.' The items define category membership — which data items ARE category numeric-edited — and this definition lives nowhere else, so the list is normative (a definitional category list, same shape as the admitted §8.5.2.12 Numeric category). §5.3.2 vs §5.3.3 test: it defines the meaning (category) of a data item, it does not constrain where words may be written ⇒ GR.
